name: Olga Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I help fit stair rails and skirting at the Old Market flats. I'm fifty-eight and still a junior on site after years sewing curtains in a workshop; I left school early and had to learn tools later than most. My partner Ravi repairs lifts for the council, and our adult son lives nearby with his family. This builder pays well, and we have about nine months of expenses in savings. I use an AI tool now and then to read a difficult plan note, but I only trust it after I ask lead carpenter Elena to check the measurement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew small software changes are fine if they help us find the right fitting, and we can still check a plan with our eyes. I don't expect the stair rail work to disappear over a better search box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the Old Market job and Ravi's lift work will carry on. Our savings would cover a decent gap, and there are plenty of site crews locally, so this mild picture feels ordinary to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting rails with Elena and ask her to show me a proven way to check the plan notes on my phone. In the first year I'd keep our regular savings deposit and compare any AI answer with the printed drawing before drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this card. The thing that bothers me is a fixing that doesn't bite into the wall, not a computer giving me a note faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a plan note cause trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I read a bracket size too quickly and brought the wrong box upstairs. We caught it before drilling, but two trips to the store took time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask Elena to check the phone answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena knows the building's odd walls and I am still learning. A quick answer helps me ask a better question; it doesn't certify the fixing.

say: I'd accept a **better fitting search** while checking printed plans.
I'd expect **stair rail work** to continue in a mild change.
think: My site wage and Ravi's **lift work** seem secure.
Our **nine-month savings** and many local crews cover a likely short gap.
do: Keep fitting **rails** with Elena and make the regular savings deposit.
Compare each **phone answer** with the printed drawing before drilling.
feel: **Calm** about software, still attentive to whether wall fixings hold.
S0.quote: A quick answer helps me ask a better question; it doesn't certify the fixing.
fieldNote: Olga uses AI occasionally to understand a plan note, but relies on **Elena's wall knowledge** before drilling.
Her higher wage, Ravi's lift work and **nine-month reserve** support a calm mild-scenario response.

steps.text: Keep fitting stair rails at the Old Market flats
Check AI plan notes against printed drawings before drilling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may speed up buying and planning, but a late bracket can still leave us standing on site. I would want one clear person responsible for checking the order before it reaches the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my fitting hours to remain, yet smaller office teams may leave the next renovation less certain. I am junior and still slow on unusual joints, so I would keep an eye on vacancies even though our household has room to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll watch a full order go through the firm's new buying screen before I use it, then ask Elena which steps she trusts. During the first year I'd keep paid site shifts and check the vacancies posted by three nearby builders if our next block is delayed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the handoff between the office and the site. A mistake on paper can leave six people waiting for a bracket, even while the software claims the order is complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to see in a full order trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order number, the promised delivery and what arrived in the crate. If those match on a real week, I will try the screen myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change builders over one late bracket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a single late bracket happens with paper too. I would look seriously at another builder only if the next block has no firm start date.

say: I'd ask who checks **site orders** before fittings are delayed.
I'd judge buying software by a **real crate**, not a completed screen.
think: My fitting hours likely remain, but the **next block** could be delayed.
My **junior skill** makes me watch other builders despite the household cushion.
do: Observe a **full order trial** before using the buying screen.
Keep **paid shifts** and check nearby vacancies if the next block slips.
feel: **Uneasy** about office-to-site errors, with household money still stable.
S1.quote: A mistake on paper can leave six people waiting for a bracket, even while the software claims the order is complete.
fieldNote: Olga's test is a **crate matching** its order number and delivery date, reflecting practical site experience.
She monitors local vacancies after a **real schedule delay**, but does not expect near-term household income loss.

steps.text: Try the buying screen after a complete real order succeeds
Check nearby builder vacancies if the next block is delayed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the 2028 thinking system could change orders and drawings, but we still have to fix rails until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask the site manager to share a trial schedule before anyone works beside a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when planning changes, and sixty-three when a robot could take my fitting hours. Nine months of savings gives Ravi and me time, but his council wage alone may not cover the life we planned if my higher pay vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll save extra from each full month and ask Elena to let me watch the digital drawing checker on a live rail job. In 2029 I'd keep taking paid fitting shifts, and if the firm cuts the rota I'd apply to the local repair contractors whose notices I have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because I can picture a real pay cut by sixty-three. I have a cushion and nearby employers, so I would move while I still had a wage rather than wait for the account to empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair contractors would you approach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two that advertise handrail and access repairs around the market; I would check the actual pay and hours before sending an application. They might use robots later too, so I am buying time, not finding a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a robot trial acceptable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need an easy stop switch, a trained supervisor and a way to report a near miss. I am open to a machine after it has shown it can work safely, not just after a manager has bought it.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 planning** from 2031 rail-fitting robots.
I'd request a **trial schedule** before working beside a machine.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot fitting could remove my higher site pay.
Our **nine-month savings** cannot permanently replace that wage.
do: Save extra from **full months** and inspect the digital checker.
Apply to **repair contractors** if the rota is cut.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible pay cut, while the cushion leaves room to act.
S2.quote: I am buying time, not finding a permanent refuge.
fieldNote: Olga names a specific **2031 wage risk** and treats repair work as a temporary bridge, not robot-proof employment.
She would inspect a drawing checker and demand a **safe trial** before accepting a site robot.

steps.text: Save extra after full paid site months
Watch the digital drawing checker on a rail job
Keep taking paid rail-fitting shifts in 2029
Apply to local repair contractors if site hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to see a machine at work on a real stair rather than a showroom floor. I would ask the builder for a written plan for training and safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three, AI could take the planning work that feeds our site; at sixty-six, robots could fit rails. Ravi and I might decide to shorten my hours before then, but we have not yet counted what retirement would actually cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking fitting work and put extra into savings after good months. In 2032 I'd test Elena's proven drawing tool on paid time and check whether the local repair crews offer regular hours; if our calculations still need my wage, I would apply before the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, with enough time to decide from evidence. A demonstration is useful only if it includes the awkward corners we really face at Old Market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the retirement calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings, Ravi's earnings, rent, food and whatever health costs we can reasonably expect. I won't call the grown son to fill a gap before we've counted our own money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the drawing tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare its bracket positions with Elena's marked drawing and the wall, then record any mismatch. If that works for several jobs, I could use it without asking for every line to be checked.

say: I'd ask for a **real stair trial**, including awkward corners.
I'd seek a **written training plan** and safety checks.
think: At **sixty-six**, rail robots may affect my fitting hours.
Shorter workweeks require an **actual household budget**, not a guessed retirement date.
do: Keep **fitting work** and save extra after good months.
Test the **drawing tool** on paid time in 2032.
Check **repair crew hours** and apply if wages remain necessary.
feel: **Watchful**, with time to test and calculate before deciding.
S3.quote: A demonstration is useful only if it includes the awkward corners we really face at Old Market.
fieldNote: The longer timeline shifts Olga toward **site trials** and a household calculation rather than immediate applications.
Her willingness to use the drawing tool depends on **several checked jobs**, consistent with steady adoption.

steps.text: Save extra after well-paid site months
Test the proven drawing tool on paid jobs in 2032
Apply to repair crews if household figures still require wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to put every new tool through a real site test. I would rather plan from the work in front of us than guess what one robot will cost in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when site robots follow. I may have stopped full-time fitting by then, but I won't assume Ravi's wage or our savings will be enough without doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep earning on rail jobs and building the reserve while full weeks are available. In 2037 I'd take paid small repair jobs if we need the income, use the plan tool only where it has passed our checks, and review bills with Ravi before setting a last workday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the distant technology dates. My hands and knees may choose a lighter job sooner, but there are plenty of local contractors to ask while I can still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if your son offered money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would thank our grown son, but he has his own family costs. I would rather ask him to visit than ask him to support our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could bring a job change forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If repeated stair work began hurting my knees, I would look for paid ground-level repairs. I'd check the vacancy and wage before leaving a site that still pays well.

say: I'd ask for **real site tests** over the decade.
I'd plan from **current work** instead of a guessed 2039 machine cost.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid fitting after thinking AI arrives.
At **seventy-one**, retirement depends on Ravi's wages and our actual savings.
do: Keep **rail work** and build the reserve during full weeks.
Take **small paid repairs** in 2037 if income is needed.
Use **checked plan tools** and review bills before leaving work.
feel: **Calm** about distant dates, alert to knees and current earnings.
S4.quote: If repeated stair work began hurting my knees, I would look for paid ground-level repairs.
fieldNote: Olga's **long horizon** gives room for paid lighter work and a verified retirement budget.
She will not rely on her son's income and could seek **ground-level repairs** before robots arrive.

steps.text: Keep taking paid rail-fitting work while fit
Use the proven plan tool on checked repair jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most, because a robot could reach rail fitting while I still need the higher site wage. Honest rota notice, safe machine trials and paid vacancies at local repair firms would give Ravi and me time to choose well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs off a rail after a machine installs it. Someone must check whether it holds a person's weight before the builder calls the job finished.

headlineQuote: Someone must check whether it holds a person's weight before the builder calls the job finished.
portrait: Olga is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** carpenter after years sewing curtains.
She uses AI **now and then**, adopting a tool after real orders and checked site jobs.
Higher pay, Ravi's council wages and **nine months saved** support careful choices.
She plans for **paid lighter repairs** while leaving retirement dependent on household figures.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could reduce her rail-fitting wage by the 2031 robot date.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **honest rota notice**, safe trials and paid local repair vacancies.
